rv.q: When the divine Mueller lets loose, you feel the earth move.
Following in the footsteps of crowd-pleasers like Jersey Boys and Motown: The Musical, this is entertaining boomer bait that elevates its by-the-numbers narrative with great songs.
What’s extraordinary is how Ms. Mueller conveys that
Mueller's engaging, moving performance here should make her one.
Snazzy stagecraft and a moving performance by Jessie Mueller help this bio-musical overcome its plodding book.
To the extent the show remains bizarrely enjoyable despite its essential hackishness, it’s this central quartet of performers who make it happen.
Beautiful, now at the Theatre, takes the early life story – and music – of the legendary singer-songwriter Carole King to create one of the most entertaining Broadway shows in years.
It's fitting that such an under-appreciated talent is represented in an extraordinary show like this one.
What she got was more complicated, and “Beautiful” does a swell job breaking it down.
Beautiful succeeds because it doesn't try to reinvent the jukebox musical so much as perfect it
Smartly, McGrath doesn’t bite off more than he can chew; the show focuses only on King’s breakthrough, when she sold her first song to Don Kirschner (Curt Bouril) to the start of her solo career.
Boomers who may not be quite as mobile as they once were will appreciate this venue as much as they will enjoy Beautiful.
Nevertheless, “Beautiful” is unusually coherent, character-driven and sincere for a jukebox musical.
It’s about the music, and only about the music that reaches us on a level we cannot verbalize.
It is a bravado performance of humility.
Mueller’s performance is destined to become one of the year's most memorable.
Criticism aside, Beautiful delivers an entertaining evening of theater, and while you may feel at times that “You’ve Lost That Lovin’ Feeling,” Jessie Mueller’s performance is, indeed, “Beautiful.”
“Beautiful” is the show for theatergoers who don’t like drama queens.
Too bad a great musical isn't only about the music.
If you go to "Beautiful" for the songs, you'll probably have a great time.
Mueller's portrayal of King — far and away the best reason to see Beautiful, which opened Sunday at Broadway's Theatre — is at once an affirmation of those virtues and a revelation.
But for those with little interest in the dramatic effectiveness of musical theatre, Beautiful certainly entertains.
Unfortunately, Douglas McGrath’s slick book reduces the storyline to a predictable soaper, and too much of the dialogue is used as intros to songs from the King canon in the manner of Mamma Mia.
As hard as Mueller works, she lacks the charisma needed to transform this kid-gloves enterprise into something, well, beautiful.
This show is so much more than just a jukebox collection of great songs.
Beautiful – The Carole King Musical, a highly pleasing trip down memory lane.
Anyone who was not a fan of King's songs before the show will most likely be one by curtain call.
If you like the music, you will probably have a good time.

cn.t: Critics praise Jessie Mueller's breakout performance, but find the formulaic book and conventional jukebox-musical structure underwhelming. The beloved songs delight, though the biographical storytelling rarely rises above slick, paint-by-numbers chronology.

sg.ra: SeatPlan and Headout consistently name Center Orchestra rows C-G as the sweet spot at this 2009 new-build Roundabout house, which was excavated up to 70 feet below street level to fit two-thirds of its seating on the orchestra level; the compressed footprint keeps C-G closer to the stage than most Broadway orchestras of equivalent row letter.

SeatPlan explicitly calls rows H-L the Orchestra's value zone, and Headout prices them around $115-120. A Sondheim-specific perk: row E was removed from the Left and Right Orchestra blocks, so SeatPlan notes row F (and by extension the H-L rows behind it) benefits from extra aisle-row stretch space. The mezz overhang does not start until around row K/L per BWW Forum and SeatPlan, so most of this band is still un-overhung.

A BWW Forum thread flags Left Orchestra row C as 'really really to the side - in an obstructed view sort of way,' and a TripAdvisor reviewer in Left Side Orchestra Row A during Beautiful reported the onstage piano blocked the right side of the stage while side-actor action on the left was cut off. Because the Sondheim auditorium was rebuilt underground in 2009 around the preserved 1918 facade, the side blocks wrap tight to the proscenium and are more angled than typical Shubert-era houses.

SeatPlan calls Center Mezzanine AA-BB 'highly prized for their unbeatable overhead views of the stage, perfect for watching a musical,' and Headout echoes that front-mezz rows are preferred over orchestra front rows by some patrons thanks to the elevation. The mezz is unusually compact here (around 328-357 seats) because the entire auditorium is an underground 2009 LEED rebuild designed by Fisher Dachs / COOKFOX with a steep modern rake, so even AA-BB feel close despite being upstairs.

SeatPlan credits the mezz's 'good rake' for letting patrons at the back still 'get a clean view down to the stage,' and Headout names rows CC and FF as value picks. Because the Sondheim was rebuilt to modern sightline specs in 2009 (Fisher Dachs, LEED-certified), there are no legacy pillars like older Shubert-era houses — obstructions here are angular (side mezz) rather than structural.
